title: A k-algebra with exactly two k-subalgebras is k x k or k[epsilon]

standard_prerequisites.name: k-subalgebras and intermediate subrings
standard_prerequisites.statement: A k-subalgebra of a k-algebra A is a subring containing k; the hypothesis is that the only such subalgebras are k and A themselves.
standard_prerequisites.use: Every contradiction in the proof is produced by exhibiting an intermediate subalgebra, at source lines 3192-3193, 3194-3195 and 3195-3196.

standard_prerequisites.name: Algebraically closed field and linear factorisation
standard_prerequisites.statement: Over an algebraically closed field k every monic polynomial factors as a product of linear factors t - a_i.
standard_prerequisites.use: The factorisation of the monic generator P is used at source lines 3194-3197, and the case distinction on the a_i decides the final shape of A.

standard_prerequisites.name: Dual numbers k[epsilon]
standard_prerequisites.statement: The k-algebra of dual numbers k[epsilon] with epsilon^2 = 0, as defined in the Varieties chapter and referred to in the surrounding text.
standard_prerequisites.use: It is one of the two possible conclusions, corresponding to a repeated root of the monic generator (source line 3198).

core_obligations: Translate the hypothesis: exactly two k-subalgebras means any subring C with k contained in C contained in A equals k or A; pick t in A outside k and conclude that A is generated by t over k, hence A is isomorphic to k[x]/I for some ideal I (source lines 3191-3193).
Exclude the case I = 0 by producing the intermediate subalgebra k[x^2], which is neither k nor A (source lines 3193-3194).

For I nonzero, let P be the monic generator of I and factor P as a product of linear factors over the algebraically closed field k; if the degree d exceeds two, exhibit the intermediate subalgebra generated by (t - a_1)(t - a_2), and for d = 2 split into distinct roots (giving k x k) and a repeated root (giving k[epsilon]) (source lines 3194-3198).

proof_roadmap.step: Turn the two-subalgebra hypothesis into k and A being the only intermediate subrings, then write A = k[x]/I using an element outside k.
Exclude I = 0 by exhibiting the forbidden intermediate subalgebra k[x^2].
Factor the monic generator, exclude degree greater than two, and read off k x k or k[epsilon] in the degree-two cases.

difficulty_reason: The counted unit is the author's own lemma lemma-no-in-between-over-k at source lines 3182-3187: if k is algebraically closed and k is contained in an algebra A which has exactly two k-subalgebras, then A is either k x k or the dual numbers k[epsilon]. The proof at source lines 3189-3199 is short but does real work: it translates the two-subalgebra hypothesis into the statement that any intermediate subring is k or A, picks an element t outside k, uses that to write A as a quotient k[x]/I, and then splits on the ideal I. The case I = 0 is excluded by exhibiting the intermediate subalgebra k[x^2]. In the remaining case the argument needs the algebraic closedness of k to factor the monic generator into linear factors, excludes degree greater than two by exhibiting the intermediate subalgebra generated by a product of two of those factors, and finally separates the two degree-two possibilities (distinct roots giving k x k, a repeated root giving k[epsilon]). Several of those steps are choices of a specific intermediate subalgebra, and the statement does not indicate them. No result outside the retained span is invoked.
